question.leadin: Answer the following about Mesopotamian empires and emperors.
question.text: This ruler of the Babylonian Empire consolidated his power and defeated Rim-Sin of Lagash. His namesake law code included the ruling "an eye for an eye".
question.clue: This Amorite king went up a mountain to receive a stele from the sun god Shamash that was later discovered in Susa.

swap.leadin: Elamite and Akkadian are among the languages that were written in this system despite not being native languages of the civilization that invented it.
swap.text: Name this writing system, developed by the Sumerians, that uses a reed stylus to make wedge-shaped impressions on clay tablets.
swap.clue: Henry Rawlinson studied the Behistun Inscription for insight into this system, which is seen on the oldest complaint tablet.

question.leadin: This region included city-states like Nineveh and Ur.
question.text: Name this region in the Middle East that gets its name from its shape and rich soil, sometimes known as the "cradle of civilization".
question.clue: This two-word English name for the "cradle of civilization" that spanned the lower Nile and Mesopotamia.

swap.leadin: The Third Dynasty of Ur rose to power after the death of this leader. --.
swap.text: Name this founder of the Akkadian Empire who conquered Uruk, Ur, and Umma.
swap.clue: He appointed his daughter Enheduanna high priestess, and his empire reached its greatest expanse under his grandson Naram-sin.

question.leadin: Amar-Sin (AA-mar-sin), Shu-Sin (SHOO-sin), and Ibbi-Sin (IB-ee-sin) all succeeded a reformer of this city's Third Dynasty named Shulgi (SHOOL-ghee).
question.text: Name this city near the mouth of the Euphrates (yoo-FRAY-teez), whose Great Ziggurat (ZIG-uh-raht) was later restored by King Nabonidus (NAA-boh-NAI-dus).
question.answerHtml: Ur [or Urim; or Uru; do not accept or prompt on “Uruk”]
question.clue: A king named -Nammu, who founded a dynasty that supplanted Lagash and the Gutians, was succeeded by Shulgi.

swap.leadin: The language spoken in this empire replaced the Sumerian language and is believed to be the earliest Semitic language.
swap.text: This Mesopotamian empire was the largest in recorded history at the time. It reached its greatest extent under the rule of Naram-Sin.
swap.clue: Its most famous ruler's life was detailed on the Ebla tablets, and started out as a cup-bearer to Ur-Zababa of Kish.

question.leadin: This empire fell to the Medes and the Babylonians in the 610 B.C. fall of Harran.
question.text: Name this empire, whose capitals included Assur ("ASS-er") and Nineveh. Tiglath-Pileser III instituted numerous reforms in this empire.
question.clue: This empire partly annexed the Kingdom of Israel under the rule of Tiglath-Pileser III ("TIG-lath pie-LEE-zur the third").

swap.text: This Assyrian capital was located on the northern part of the Tigris.
swap.clue: This city was sacked by a coalition including Scythians assembled in 612 BC by the Median king Cyaxares ("kye-ax-AIR-ees"), ending the dominance of a line that included Tiglath-Pileser III.

question.leadin: A magnificent blue and gold copy of this structure can be found opposite the Market gate of Miletus in the Pergamon Museum.
question.text: Name this gate that was once built into the wall that surrounded Babylon. It is named for a deity.
question.clue: This large blue and gold structure located in Babylon. The walls lining the street leading up to this structure were decorated with a brick mosaic of lions and flowers.

swap.text: Fragments of Hammurabi's Code have been found in this city, whose "scribal corner" is rich with ancient texts. Various Mesopotamian dynasties sought to control this city of religious importance, the home of the god Enlil.
swap.clue: The best example of a Sumerian schoolhouse was found in this city, which was the center of worship for Enlil. This city's Ekur Temple was rebuilt by Naram-Sin.

question.text: This warrior king from the north invaded Sumer beginning around 2340 BCE, creating a unified empire there for the first time.
question.clue: This ruler famously defeated Lugal-Zage-Si of Umma, the last Sumerian King.

swap.text: The Gutians ended the reign of this kingdom, which was most famously ruled by Sargon.
swap.clue: This native language of the Assyrian and Babylonian empires. It was spoken in a namesake empire founded by Sargon over four thousand years ago.

question.text: While conducting excavations in Assyria, Layard found many of these statues of winged human headed bulls, which were often found in pairs at the entrances of buildings. Their male counterparts are called shedu.
question.clue: Several Mesopotamian empires, but most notably the Assyrians, built statues of these protective creatures with a person's face, eagle's wings, and the body of either a bull or a lion.

swap.leadin: Invading Egypt sure can get messy.
swap.text: According to Herodotus, the invasion of Egypt by this empire's king Sennacherib was stymied when mice ate the bowstrings of his army. This empire with capital at Nineveh was later ruled by Ashurbanipal.
swap.clue: A king of this empire built an elaborate palace at Khorsabad called Dur-Sharrukin, whose gate included carvings of winged bulls with human-faces called lamassu.

question.leadin: The oldest known notation of music is a series of songs written in this language, found in the city of Ugarit.
question.text: Name this language spoken in the kingdom of Mittani. The speakers of this language likely shared ancestry with Urartu in modern day Armenia.
question.clue: This ethnic group largely made up the population of the Mitanni Kingdom to the southeast of the Hittite Empire. Kikkuli ("kee-KOO-lee") wrote a horse training manual in this ethnic group's namesake language, which was most closely related to Urartian.

swap.text: At Ur, Woolley excavated one of these structures, whose construction was begun by Ur-Nammu. The White Temple at Uruk was built on one of these structures, which have multiple tiers of receding size.
swap.clue: Koldewey also found one that he took to be a temple to Marduk, the name of which, Etemenanki, translates as "The Foundation of Heaven and Earth."

question.leadin: He destroyed Susa after conquering the Elamites and sacked Babylon after his brother, Shamash-shum-ukin, rebelled against him.
question.text: Name this Assyrian ruler, who came to the throne when Esarhaddon died in Egypt.
question.clue: One relief from this man's palace shows his queen sitting in front of him while he reclines; that relief is in a garden with a rebel's severed head.

swap.leadin: Dominant rulers gradually claimed this title instead of ensi, which kings of Isin and Larsa took as pious stewards of a temple's farmlands.
swap.text: Give this Sumerian title that precedes "Anne-Mundu" to identify a "king of the four corners" from Adab, "Zage-Si" to identify a warlord overthrown by Sargon, and "banda" to identify a mythical king of Uruk.

question.leadin: Identify the following about the ancient Middle East, FTPE.
question.text: Muwatalli's children both had Hurrian names, perhaps due to the influence of this northern Mesopotamian kingdom with capital at Washshukanni that lasted from 1500 BC to 1280 BC.
question.clue: Based on terms in the Kikkuli horse-training manual, the names of several rulers, and a list of deities found in a treaty, the rulers of this polity are argued to have been Indo-Europeans.

swap.leadin: The only woman attested to in this document is Kug-Bu, the Tavern Keeper.
swap.text: Name this compendium of rulers that includes five dynasties of Kish and three dynasties of Ur.
